stimulus.text: "I left these shores a red-hot imperialist. I wanted the American eagle to go screaming into the Pacific. … But I have thought some more, since then, and I have seen that we do not intend to free, but to subjugate the people of the Philippines. … It should, it seems to me, be our pleasure and duty to make these people free, and let them deal with their own domestic questions in their own way. And so I am an anti-imperialist. I am opposed to having the eagle put its talons on any other land." — Mark Twain, quoted in the New York World, October 15, 1900

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from Mark Twain, quoted in the New York World, October 15, 1900, public domain.
stem: Twain's argument most directly agrees with which other anti-imperialist claim?

options.text: Colonies would bring cheap labor that undercut American workers
options.misconception: That is the labor objection to empire. Twain's argument is about liberty and consent, not about wages.

options.text: Ruling a foreign people without their consent betrays republican ideals
The Philippines were too far away for the navy to defend
options.misconception: Distance and defense are strategic worries. Twain's argument is moral, not strategic.

options.text: Missionaries should convert Filipinos before annexation
options.misconception: That is a pro-imperialist missionary position. Twain opposes annexation itself, not its timing.

rationales.A: That is the labor objection to empire. Twain's argument is about liberty and consent, not about wages.
rationales.B: Twain calls American rule subjugation and demands freedom. Background: the League said the same, that ruling a people without consent betrays the republic's ideals.
rationales.C: Distance and defense are strategic worries. Twain's argument is moral, not strategic.
rationales.D: That is a pro-imperialist missionary position. Twain opposes annexation itself, not its timing.
rationales.general:
1. Name Twain's core claim. Ruling Filipinos against their will is subjugation, not freedom.
2. Ask which League claim matches it. Background: the League said holding colonies betrayed the republic's founding ideals.
3. Test the rest. Labor, distance, and missionaries are real debate points, but none of them is Twain's point here.
4. Put it together. Twain and the League share one argument: consent is what makes rule legitimate.
Remember: different objections to one policy are not the same objection, so match the reason, not just the side.
